title: Affordable preservation and recovery of exceptional plant diversity

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an affordable, broadly transferable way to preserve exceptional plants at ultralow temperatures and reliably regenerate healthy plants afterward. Exceptional species include plants whose seeds are scarce, short-lived or sensitive to drying, making conventional seed banking impractical or impossible. Depending on the species, preservation may use embryonic axes or cultured tissues rather than whole seeds.

The central ambition is predictable conservation across difficult species and across multiple genetically representative individuals within each species. Preserving one successful clone does not capture a species’ genetic diversity. A useful system would combine reliable preservation, regeneration and management of many distinct genetic lines, using a small enough set of protocols to make conservation feasible beyond specialist laboratories.

significance.text: Broadly reproducible preservation and recovery could substantially expand the plant diversity that conservation institutions can securely bank. For exceptional species excluded from conventional seed storage, living collections and cryopreservation are primary options for conservation outside their natural habitats. The transformative advance would be making reliable recovery affordable across diverse taxa and representative individuals, extending existing species-specific successes into a much broader conservation capability.

The direct consequence would be access to living plants regenerated from stored genetic resources, with secure duplication potentially allowing institutions to safeguard material at more than one facility. Preserving multiple representative lines would also retain more within-species variation than banking a single clone. These benefits depend on successful recovery and retained genetic and reproductive integrity; survival of some cells alone would not establish conservation success.

Conditional downstream possibility: recovered plants could support population reinforcement, reintroduction and research, but a banked collection would not itself establish a self-sustaining wild population. Restoration would still require suitable habitat, appropriate genetic composition and, where relevant, ecological partners. The conservation impact would therefore depend on how the stored diversity is used alongside wider ecological work.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a broadly applicable, economical route from diverse starting material to reliably recoverable plants. The 2024 review explicitly asks whether widely applicable protocols can be developed through systematic evaluation of sensitivity to osmotic, temperature and chemical stresses. A protocol optimized for one species or genotype does not demonstrate that transferability.

The biological barriers span preservation and recovery. Intracellular ice can damage cellular structures and trigger cell death, while the preparation and preservation process exposes tissues to additional stresses. Material that survives must still resume organized growth and regenerate a healthy plant. Species-specific culture requirements, including particularly difficult culture and cryopreservation of some tropical trees, make this a coupled cryobiology and regeneration problem.

Conservation at scale adds a separate burden: initiating, identifying, preserving and recovering multiple lines from a genetically representative group of individuals. The engineering challenge includes standardized procedures, secure duplicate storage and practical economics. Success with a single easily cultured line would leave both genetic representation and the cost of maintaining many lines unresolved.

current_state.text: The documented baseline is the review by Nagel, Pence, Ballesteros and colleagues, “Plant Cryopreservation: Principles, Applications, and Challenges of Banking Plant Diversity at Ultralow Temperatures,” first published on 11 January 2024, DOI 10.1146/annurev-arplant-070623-103551. As described in the supplied evidence review, its printed pages 808–810 document established crop collections and smaller-scale banking of wild species. Cryopreservation is therefore an existing conservation practice; the proposed advance concerns its breadth, predictability, genetic coverage and affordability.

Printed pages 810–811 identify the larger unfinished task for exceptional wild species. Banking multiple genetic lines had been reported for a few wild species but was not widely implemented across the many species requiring tissue cryopreservation. The review also describes difficult species-specific culture and recovery, particularly for tropical trees. These findings establish meaningful progress alongside substantial scaling barriers; the supplied evidence does not provide a defensible numerical measure of overall species coverage, recovery rates or costs.

Evidence boundary: the supplied assessment reports an identity-verified, complete main article through printed page 824, with no extraction truncation. Separately referenced supplementary materials were not supplied. No search entries or later studies were provided to establish developments through 1 November 2026, so the 2024 findings should not be read as a verified account of everything achieved by that later date. This freshness limitation does not invalidate the dated achievements or demonstrate that subsequent advances did not occur.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent facilities would apply a small, explicitly defined set of protocols to a large, taxonomically diverse panel of difficult exceptional species, including multiple genetically representative individuals per species. The evaluation would state how species and individuals were selected, distinguish shared procedures from species-specific adjustments, and report failures alongside successes. A finite panel would establish demonstrated breadth and transferability, without proving literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent facilities preserve diverse exceptional species using few defined protocols

completion_criteria.text: Proposed recovery criteria: after defined storage periods and interfacility transfer, facilities would recover healthy plants capable of reproduction appropriate to the species’ normal biology. Evaluation would follow development beyond initial tissue survival or early regrowth and assess genetic integrity and retained representation of the original collection. A universal requirement for fertile seed production would be inappropriate for species that naturally produce few or no viable seeds.
completion_criteria.label: Stored and transferred material regenerates healthy, reproductively capable plants

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical criteria: before testing, investigators would specify species-appropriate success thresholds for recovery, health, reproductive performance and genetic integrity, together with an explicit affordability target. Reports would include recovery rates by species and line, losses of representation, storage duration, repeatability between facilities, and costs of establishing, storing, transferring and recovering material. The tested storage periods and operating conditions would bound the result; these proposed criteria are not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Report prespecified success thresholds, affordability targets and full resource costs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BOT-04, “An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants,” has the closest technical overlap because reliable regeneration across diverse plants is central to both concepts. BOT-09 adds preservation, recovery after storage and representative genetic banking; it does not require genome editing. BOT-05, “Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance,” could help explain differences in tissue response and recovery, but predictive whole-plant biology is a broader objective than a demonstrated conservation protocol.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-07, “Transferable resurrection-like desiccation tolerance in productive crops,” overlaps through cellular responses to water loss and preservation stress. Its target is tolerance in productive plants, whereas BOT-09 seeks recoverable stored material and can include species intrinsically sensitive to drying. BOT-06, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major crop families,” concerns producing clonal offspring through seeds. BOT-09 may store clonal tissues, but conserving many distinct genetic lines remains necessary to represent diversity.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-14, “Programmable, multigenerational epigenetic inheritance of adaptive plant traits,” concerns controlling inherited states; BOT-09 instead needs to assess whether preservation and regeneration retain the biological properties relevant to conservation. BOT-12, “A causal map of plant-wide communication and plasmodesmatal control,” BOT-13, “A predictive mechanism for plant cell-wall growth and mechanical sensing,” and BOT-17, “Predictive control of plant cell-division planes and tissue patterning,” could inform mechanisms of organized recovery, but each remains a distinct mechanistic objective rather than a requirement to solve all of plant regeneration.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-16, “Predictable control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange,” intersects with the ecological conditions that may matter when recovered plants are returned to habitats. That relationship reinforces the boundary between successful banking and successful restoration. BOT-09 remains a preservation and recovery capability; controlling ecological partnerships is a separate innovation.

change_log.change: Retained BOT-09’s identity and expanded the explanation of exceptional species, eligible tissues and representative genetic lines.
change_log.reason: The review clarifies that the scope includes scarce, short-lived and desiccation-sensitive seeds, embryonic axes and cultured tissues, and conservation beyond a single clone.

change_log.change: Separated established cryopreservation practice from the proposed broadly transferable, affordable capability.
change_log.reason: Existing crop collections and wild-species successes support the foundation without establishing the full innovation.

change_log.change: Dated the evidence baseline to the January 2024 review and preserved uncertainty about developments through November 2026.
change_log.reason: The supplied record contains no later search findings establishing how far the barriers had changed.

change_log.change: Integrated ice damage, osmotic, temperature and chemical stresses, culture requirements and genetic-line management into the missing breakthrough.
change_log.reason: These are distinct biological and operational barriers identified in the supplied review.

change_log.change: Replaced a universal fertility requirement with normal reproductive capacity appropriate to each species.
change_log.reason: Exceptional species may naturally produce few or no viable seeds, making universal fertile-seed recovery an unsuitable criterion.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to cover independent replication, defined storage periods, interfacility transfer, recovery rates, genetic integrity, representation and costs.
change_log.reason: The original proposal left breadth, affordability and recovery insufficiently operationalized. The expanded criteria remain proposals rather than published standards.

change_log.change: Separated direct conservation benefits from conditional restoration outcomes and added distinct roster relationships.
change_log.reason: Recovered plants do not establish self-sustaining populations, and overlap with regeneration, stress tolerance or ecological partnerships does not make those innovations interchangeable.

change_log.change: Preserved the complete-main-text and unavailable-supplement distinction.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports main-article findings without establishing inspection of supplementary material.

unresolved_issues: Developments after the documented 2024 baseline, including the extent of progress by 1 November 2026, remain unverified in the supplied record.
The species panel, sampling strategy and number of representative individuals needed per species remain to be specified.
The acceptable amount of species-specific adjustment within a small transferable protocol set remains undefined.
Affordability targets, storage durations and species-appropriate recovery, reproductive and genetic-integrity thresholds remain proposed rather than settled.
The supplied evidence does not establish aggregate numerical coverage, recovery performance or practical costs across exceptional species.
Separately referenced supplementary materials were unavailable in the supplied assessment; no conclusions here resolve questions dependent on those materials.

brief.title: Affordable plant preservation and regrowth
possible: Conservation teams could store plants whose seeds are too scarce, short-lived or sensitive to drying for ordinary seed banks. They could preserve plant tissues at extremely low temperatures, then reliably grow healthy plants from them using affordable methods that work across many difficult species.
why: More of the plant world could enter long-term conservation collections. Keeping material from genetically different individuals would protect variation within each species, while duplicate collections at separate facilities would provide backups.
Recovered plants could support research, reinforce threatened populations and help return species to places where they have disappeared.

sources.who: Manuela Nagel, Valerie Pence, Daniel Ballesteros and colleagues
sources.showed: Their review describes established frozen crop collections and smaller collections of wild species. Storing genetically different individuals remains uncommon across wild species that need tissue storage, and growing plants after storage can be difficult.
sources.quote:
Later, in vitro cultured flax cells were successfully preserved by slow-cooling techniques that were
introduced in 1968 ( 111).
sources.cited_for: The review establishes existing preservation successes and the barriers to extending them across difficult species.
sources.not_established: Existing collections do not establish affordable, reliable preservation and regrowth across diverse species and representative individuals.

sources.who: Carla Benelli, Waed Tarraf and colleagues
sources.showed: The team established a frozen conservation collection for the endangered Sicilian fir using pollen, embryos—the young plants inside seeds—and tissues grown in culture. Recovery varied between trees.
sources.quote: to establish the first cryobank of this endangered species in Polizzi Generosa (Palermo, Italy), inside the ‘Madonie Regional Park’.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates preservation of different kinds of material from an endangered tree, with uneven recovery.
sources.not_established: This species-specific study does not establish transferable methods or healthy, reproductively capable plants after storage and transfer.

shown: Nagel and colleagues describe established frozen crop collections and smaller wild-plant collections. Banking genetically different individuals has succeeded for a few wild species. Benelli and colleagues established a collection for Sicilian fir, but recovery varied between trees.
missing: A small set of affordable methods has yet to work reliably across many difficult species and genetically representative individuals.
Stored tissues must reliably grow into healthy plants that retain their genetic makeup and can reproduce as their species normally does.
Independent facilities have yet to demonstrate repeatable recovery after storage and transfer while accounting for all costs and losses.

milestones.label: Different facilities preserve diverse species with few shared methods
milestones.explanation: Independent facilities would have to preserve a diverse panel of difficult species and representative individuals using few defined methods, reporting failures and adjustments. This would establish how broadly the methods transfer.

milestones.label: Stored and transferred material becomes healthy plants that reproduce
milestones.explanation: After defined storage periods and transfer between facilities, material would have to yield healthy plants with normal reproduction, genetic makeup and collection diversity retained. This would establish recovery beyond tissue survival.

milestones.label: Results meet declared recovery and affordability targets
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to set recovery, health, reproduction, genetic and affordability targets beforehand, then report results, losses, repeatability and all resource costs. This would establish practical performance under tested conditions.

uncertain: Which species and how many genetically different individuals would provide a convincing test of breadth?
How much adjustment for individual species can a shared method allow before it loses its practical advantage?
Suitable storage periods, affordability targets and standards for healthy recovery and retained genetic diversity remain unsettled.
